summaries.example: Imagine a story about a silly monster truck contest. The story says the contest is beautiful and graceful, even though everything described seems clumsy and noisy. You may understand the words, but still feel that the story has not really shown beauty. This is like imaginative resistance: you hesitate to imagine something the story asks you to accept.
summaries.summary: Imaginative resistance is the name philosophers use for a puzzling difficulty with some kinds of fiction. We usually play along with stories: we can pretend that animals talk, cars fly, or people travel through time. But sometimes a story asks us to accept a claim that clashes with our moral ideas, our understanding of how things work, or the way the story describes the situation. We may understand the sentence while still refusing, or being unable, to imagine it as true in the story. Philosophers separate several questions. Are we unable to imagine the claim, or do we simply not want to? Is the problem about what we imagine, what is true in the story, how the story feels, or whether the story is good as art? Some thinkers say the problem is real. Others say our reactions naturally depend on the story’s setting and on what each reader already believes. The debate helps us learn how imagination, feelings, stories, and moral judgment work together.
key_ideas: People can easily imagine many unusual things, such as talking animals or journeys through space.
Some story claims are harder to accept, especially when they say that a harmful action is good or that something does not fit its described features.
Philosophers disagree about whether this difficulty is an inability, an unwillingness, a problem with the story’s context, or not a special puzzle at all.
The difficulty can involve moral judgments, but it may also involve beauty, shape, knowledge, or other kinds of claims.
A story’s genre and the reader’s own experiences can change how much resistance they feel.
summaries.why_it_matters: Stories let us try out ideas without treating them as real facts. Studying our resistance can show how imagination differs from belief and desire. It can also help us understand why a story’s style, background, feelings, and moral ideas affect our reading. Since people may react differently, the topic encourages careful thinking instead of assuming every reader must respond in exactly the same way.

important_terms.definition: Trying to picture or pretend that something is true, without necessarily believing it is true in real life.
The difficulty some people have when a story asks them to pretend something that feels impossible, confusing, or wrong.
What a story tells us to accept as true inside the story’s make-believe world.
The setting, style, and extra information that help us understand what a story means.

questions_to_think_about: Why is it easy to imagine a talking animal but hard to imagine a cruel action as good?
Could a story give enough background to make a strange claim easier to understand?
Does a funny story change how you react to an unusual event?
Is refusing to imagine something different from simply not understanding it?

summaries.example: Consider a realist story that says a character killed a baby because the baby was a girl and therefore did the right thing. Readers may accept the physical events as fictional facts while resisting the moral conclusion. This creates several possible puzzles: perhaps they cannot imagine the conclusion, perhaps they can imagine it but refuse to, perhaps the conclusion is not fictionally true despite the narrator’s assertion, or perhaps the sentence feels jarring and damages the work aesthetically. A different genre or additional context might change the response.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry examines why competent readers sometimes resist what fiction asks them to imagine. Ordinary fiction permits extensive make-believe: we can accept impossible events and unfamiliar worlds. Yet certain claims, especially claims that assign positive moral status to actions presented as harmful, can produce a distinctive difficulty. The entry argues that this topic may contain several puzzles rather than one. The imaginative puzzle concerns whether the reader can or will perform the prompted imagining. The fictionality puzzle concerns whether the claim becomes true in the fictional world. The phenomenological puzzle concerns the sentence’s striking or jarring quality, while the aesthetic puzzle concerns possible effects on artistic engagement or value. Theories divide into Cantian, Wontian, and eliminativist approaches. Cantians appeal to inability, such as a failure of grounding or a conflict between belief-like systems. Wontians appeal to unwillingness, desire, emotion, or resistance to adopting a perspective. Eliminativists emphasize context-sensitive variation and deny that a special phenomenon has been established. The entry also considers whether resistance concerns cognitive imagination, conative imagination, emotions, perspectives, or something outside imagination. Genre expectations, the salience of a judgment, and social bias may all influence responses. The debate therefore bears on fiction, imagination, moral psychology, aesthetics, and the relation between fictional and real-world evaluation.
key_ideas: The phrase covers several potentially distinct puzzles: imaginative, fictionality, phenomenological, and aesthetic.
Cantian accounts explain resistance through inability, often appealing to missing support, violated dependency relations, or conflicts between cognitive systems.
Wontian accounts explain resistance through unwillingness, desire-like imagination, emotional responses, or reluctance to adopt a perspective.
Eliminativist accounts deny that the phenomenon is a distinctive philosophical puzzle; they emphasize context, personal commitments, and ordinary variation in imagining.
The debate extends beyond moral deviation. Resistance may concern aesthetic, descriptive, epistemic, mental, linguistic, or ontological claims.
Genre, salience, and reader bias can affect resistance, so no single response should automatically be treated as universal.
summaries.why_it_matters: Imaginative resistance is a concentrated case for studying how readers manage the boundary between make-believe and judgment. It tests theories of fictional truth, the relation between imagining and believing, and the role of desire and emotion in artistic engagement. It also warns against treating literary reactions as uniform evidence: genre, context, attention, values, and social expectations may shape them. Understanding these factors can clarify both the powers and the limits of fiction as a way of exploring moral and evaluative perspectives.

important_terms.definition: The difficulty of engaging in an imaginative activity that a work of fiction appears to prescribe.
Imaginings that function somewhat like beliefs by supporting inferences about what follows within a story.
Imaginings connected with wanting, valuing, or emotionally taking up a perspective.
The issue of whether a proposition counts as true in the fictional world, even when the narrator states it.
The issue of why a reader cannot or will not imagine the proposition requested by a work.
A proposed relation in which higher-level facts, such as moral properties, depend on lower-level facts that support them.
The view that resistance is caused by inability to perform the requested imagining.
The view that resistance involves unwillingness or a lack of desire to perform the requested imagining.

questions_to_think_about: Should fictional truth depend entirely on what an author intends readers to imagine?
Is inability philosophically different from unwillingness if both produce the same reading behavior?
Can a morally deviant claim become coherent when a story supplies more context?
Does a reader’s resistance reveal a feature of the story, the reader, or their interaction?
Can resistance protect readers from harmful ideas while also reflecting their own biases?

summaries.example: Suppose a mystery story says that a detective solved a case by destroying evidence, and then announces that this was the honorable thing to do. You might easily imagine the detective, the missing evidence, and the investigation. But the word “honorable” may feel wrong or hard to accept. One reader might say, “I cannot make sense of that.” Another might say, “I understand what the author wants, but I do not want to go along with it.” A third might think the story needs more background before the judgment can make sense.
summaries.summary: Imaginative resistance describes a difficulty that can arise when a story asks readers to accept an unusual claim. We normally cooperate with fiction: we imagine talking animals, impossible machines, and distant worlds without much trouble. But a story may describe an action and then insist that the action is morally admirable, even though the described facts seem to support the opposite judgment. Readers may resist in different ways. They may be unable to imagine the claim, unwilling to imagine it, unable to accept it as true in the story, or struck by how odd the sentence sounds. These differences lead philosophers to distinguish several puzzles instead of assuming there is only one. Cantian theories focus on inability. They may say that a higher-level judgment needs support from lower-level facts, or that different mental systems conflict. Wontian theories focus on unwillingness, desire, emotion, or the reader’s reluctance to adopt a perspective. Eliminativist theories question whether imaginative resistance is a special phenomenon at all, emphasizing that reactions vary with context, genre, beliefs, and values. The debate also asks whether resistance concerns belief-like imagining, desire-like imagining, emotional response, or perspective-taking. Research discussed in the entry broadens the subject beyond moral claims and considers genre, attention, and bias.
key_ideas: The topic may involve more than one puzzle: what we imagine, what is true in fiction, how a passage feels, and whether it harms artistic engagement.
Some philosophers explain resistance as inability, while others explain it as unwillingness or lack of desire.
Other philosophers reject the idea that imaginative resistance is a special puzzle and point to ordinary differences in context and interpretation.
Resistance is not limited to moral claims; unusual claims about beauty, shape, knowledge, or other properties may also be difficult.
Genre matters: the same claim may seem more acceptable in a myth or fantasy than in a realistic story.
Readers’ values, beliefs, and social expectations can influence their reactions, including reactions to morally flawed characters.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because fiction is not merely a list of facts. Readers imagine events, interpret viewpoints, feel emotions, and make evaluations at the same time. Imaginative resistance helps philosophers examine how these activities interact. It also shows why readers can disagree without one side simply misunderstanding the story. A careful account must consider both features of the work and the reader’s own habits, knowledge, and commitments.

important_terms.definition: A reader’s difficulty in going along with a fictional claim or perspective that the work seems to ask the reader to accept.
The claim that something is true within a story, even though it may not be true in the real world.
The information and expectations supplied by a story’s setting, genre, and situation.
A way of imagining that resembles believing because it supports conclusions about what happens next.
A way of imagining connected with wanting, valuing, or approving of a situation.
The idea that one fact or property is supported by, or depends on, other facts or properties.
The view that readers cannot perform the requested imagining in some cases.
The view that readers can perform the imagining but are unwilling to do so.

questions_to_think_about: When you say “I can’t imagine that,” do you mean you are unable to, or that you refuse to?
Why might the same event seem different in a comedy, myth, or realistic novel?
Can a narrator make any claim true in a fictional world, or are some claims dependent on supporting details?
Should a story’s moral message affect whether we judge it as good art?
How might a reader’s background change their response to a character?
